title: Nala and Damayanti
hook: Kali arrives too late for the swayamvara, waits for one small lapse, and enters Nala
carry: one small habit of care, done on purpose

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nala and Damayanti met in the middle of a test: he carried the gods' message honestly, and she chose the one who blinked. Did you notice a human sign in someone? Day seven hundred ninety.

On their way home from the wedding, the gods meet latecomers on the road. One is Kali, the spirit of strife and bad luck, with his companion Dvapara. Kali is hurrying to the swayamvara to win Damayanti. The gods tell him he's missed it: she has chosen Nala. Kali doesn't take it well. He swears to get into Nala, to take his kingdom, to part him from his wife, and he tells Dvapara to get into the dice. Then he does something quietly frightening. He waits.
screen: `THE LATECOMERS ON THE ROAD.` → `KALI'S OATH.` → `HE WAITS.`

segments.voice: Nala, the story says, is a good king. He rules well, he offers sacrifices, he loves Damayanti, and they have children. Kali can't find a way in. So he watches, and he waits, for a long, long time. Then one evening Nala relieves himself and, before he sits down for his evening prayers, forgets to wash his feet. That's all. One small lapse in a careful life. And through it, Kali enters him. Kali goes to Nala's brother, Pushkara, and whispers to him: challenge Nala at dice, and you'll win his kingdom. And Nala, with Kali inside him, can't say no to the challenge. They play. Nala loses. They play again. He loses again. His ministers come to the door to stop him. The people of the city come. Damayanti herself comes. He won't even look up. So Damayanti does the one thing in her power. She calls the charioteer, Varshneya, and has him take their children away to her father's house, where they'll be safe. Then Nala loses everything else. And here Pushkara asks for one more stake: Damayanti. Nala won't do it. He stands up, takes off his ornaments, and walks out of his own city in a single cloth. Damayanti walks after him. Remember who is listening. Yudhishthira, the king who also played and couldn't stop, sits there in the forest and hears all of this. The sage doesn't point at him. He doesn't have to. A story about someone else lets a person look at his own life without being shamed.
screen: `KALI WAITS FOR ONE LAPSE.` · `PUSHKARA'S CHALLENGE.` · `THE CHILDREN SENT AWAY.` · then, large: `NALA WON'T STAKE DAMAYANTI.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Think of one small habit of care in your own day: brushing your teeth, locking the door, saying goodnight, taking a moment before a meal. Something small that keeps things in order. Breathe in, and see yourself doing it. Breathe out, and let a little respect go toward that ordinary habit. In this story, one forgotten habit opened a door. That's a reason to notice, not to worry. Just honor the small things for a moment. If you pray, you can bring your daily habits into your prayer. If not, simply rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kali. The spirit of strife who waits years for one small opening, a forgotten washing, before he enters a good king and will not let the dice stop.
Your line: one small habit of care, done on purpose. Today, do one small habit of care slowly and on purpose, and notice what it protects. Day seven hundred ninety.

howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, the sage Brihadashva narrates Nala's loss at dice to Yudhishthira; in that telling, Kali gets in through a small ritual lapse, feet left unwashed before the evening rite.

original.note: Sanskrit Kali (with short vowels), the spirit of strife and bad luck in this story, not the goddess Kālī.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nala was just a reckless gambler.
what it means: in the story, Kali enters him through one small lapse, and he can't stop playing.
what a scholar hears: Kali here is a personified force of strife, and his name differs from the goddess Kālī's in its vowel lengths.
recall: warned the game would bring quarrel

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: Kali and Dvapara meet the gods; Kali enters Nala; Pushkara's dice game; the children sent away; Nala leaves the city)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the lapse (Nala neglects to wash his feet before the evening rite) and that Kali waits a long time; Ganguli gives a span of years, left without a number.
Confirm Varshneya takes the children to Damayanti's father's house in Vidarbha.
Confirm Pushkara asks Nala to stake Damayanti and that Nala refuses.
Kali (कलि, the personified Kali age/strife) vs. the goddess Kālī (काली): the original and trapdoor make this distinction; confirm wording.
The teach notes Yudhishthira is listening; it makes no claim about what he feels.
Editor: corrected the Kali/Kālī vowel note (kali has two short vowels; Kālī has two long ones), in the original note and trapdoor.
Audit: howItsDone no longer makes an unsourced claim about what retellings keep; practice line no longer tells the listener what not to feel.
